channel.title: Finding issues in the database on Splunk Observability Cloud Workshops
channel.description: Recent content in Finding issues in the database on Splunk Observability Cloud Workshops

item.title: 1. The Problem
item.description:
“Why are recommendations taking so long?” #

Customers can browse the Astronomy Shop, but product recommendations sometimes take several seconds to appear. The page eventually returns results, and the requests may show no errors. From the customer’s perspective, though, the shop feels slow.

The recommendation service retrieves product information from PostgreSQL. Somewhere along that path, a request is doing more work than expected. A successful response tells us the request completed; it does not tell us whether the database handled it efficiently.

item.title: 2. Follow the Slow Request
item.description:
Start with the customer symptom: recommendations sometimes take too long to appear. APM helps locate the dependency contributing to that delay.

Exercise · Locate the slow database call
  1. Open APM Overview and set the environment to [NAME OF WORKSHOP]-workshop.
  2. Open the Service Map and locate the recommendation service.
  3. Find its connection to the PostgreSQL database, shown as postgresql:astroshop in the example.
  4. Select that connection and inspect its latency and request/error charts.

item.title: 3. Find the Expensive Query
item.description:
Database Monitoring lets you move from an instance-level view to the queries responsible for its workload.

Exercise · Identify the recommendation query

  1. From the APM service map, open APM → Database Monitoring → Overview. Filter to PostgreSQL and your workshop environment, keeping the same time window.

  2. Select the PostgreSQL database for your workshop. Under Database Instances on the right, select the database instance. If there is more than one, select the one with the longest average duration.

item.title: 4. Understand the Execution Plan
item.description:
A normalized query replaces literal values with placeholders such as ?, making it easier to group similar statements. An execution plan describes how PostgreSQL processes a query: reading tables, combining rows, sorting, and returning results.

Exercise · Follow the work through the plan
  1. Read the Query statement at the top of the details pane. Identify products, product_tags, the category and tag filters, and the ordering by relevance score.
  2. Inspect the JOIN condition. How are the tables related?
  3. Open the Explain plans tab, select the plan if needed, and switch between the List and Graph views. Which nodes account for most of the plan cost?

item.title: 5. Investigate with AI Assistance
item.description:
Use AI assistance to explain the query and develop a remediation proposal. Compare its suggestions with the SQL and plan you just inspected.

Exercise · Summarize and evaluate the query

  1. In Query statement, select Summarize.

  2. Read the Query summarization panel. Explain in your own words what the query is intended to return: products, tags, and relevance scores filtered by category and tag, ordered for recommendations.

item.title: 6. Root Cause and Wrap-Up
item.description:
You have followed a slow application dependency into the database and identified the work behind it. Turn that evidence into a useful handoff to the development team.

Exercise · Write your incident handoff

Using your observations, prepare a short explanation that includes:

  1. Symptom: Which service and database dependency were slow, in which environment and time window?
  2. Evidence: Which query did you identify, what was its observed duration, and what did the plan reveal? Label estimates as estimates.
  3. Root cause: Explain how the missing product-to-tag join relationship creates a Cartesian product and increases the work before the final limit.
  4. Proposed fix: Restore the intended join predicate, then review additional tuning suggestions with the database owner.
  5. Validation: Describe how you would test result correctness and compare query duration, intermediate rows, execution plans, and application latency under comparable load after the fix.

What we learned #

Investigation step What it established
APM service map The recommendation service had a slow PostgreSQL dependency.
Database Monitoring queries A product recommendation query took seconds per execution.
SQL and execution plan The missing join relationship produced excessive intermediate combinations and an expensive sort.
AI assistance AI suggested a join correction and additional tuning ideas to assess.
Validation plan How to check correctness and measure improvement before declaring the incident resolved.

Congratulations
